results.name: participant_yes_rate_sd
results.description: Standard deviation across participants (a new participant starts whenever trial_index resets downward) of the overall yes-rate; observed > null means people differ in response bias/generalisation breadth more than the model's single shared parameter set implies.
results.code:
# name: participant_yes_rate_sd
# description: Standard deviation across participants (a new participant starts whenever trial_index resets downward) of the overall yes-rate; observed > null means people differ in response bias/generalisation breadth more than the model's single shared parameter set implies.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].astype(int)
    pid = (ti.diff() < 0).cumsum()
    rates = df["rating"].astype(float).groupby(pid).mean()
    return float(rates.std()) if len(rates) > 1 else 0.0

results.name: four_example_far_target_yes_rate
results.description: For 4-example sets, yes-rate on targets more than 20 outside [min,max] of the examples (excluding targets <=10 and target 100); observed > null means the model under-produces far generalisation once four examples establish a rule (people extend well-supported rules across magnitudes more than the model's interval mass allows).
results.code:
# name: four_example_far_target_yes_rate
# description: For 4-example sets, yes-rate on targets more than 20 outside [min,max] of the examples (excluding targets <=10 and target 100); observed > null means the model under-produces far generalisation once four examples establish a rule (people extend well-supported rules across magnitudes more than the model's interval mass allows).
def test_statistic(df):
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",").apply(lambda l: [int(x) for x in l])
    k = sets.str.len().to_numpy()
    mn = sets.apply(min).to_numpy(); mx = sets.apply(max).to_numpy()
    dist = np.maximum(0, np.maximum(mn - t, t - mx))
    m = (k == 4) & (dist > 20) & (t > 10) & (t < 100)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy()
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: within_block_position_gain
results.description: Within runs of consecutive trials showing the same set (run length >= 4), yes-rate on the 4th-and-later targets minus yes-rate on the first target of the run; observed > null means people grow more liberal as they keep answering about the same set (warm-up/anchoring), which the trial-independent model does not produce beyond stimulus differences.
results.code:
# name: within_block_position_gain
# description: Within runs of consecutive trials showing the same set (run length >= 4), yes-rate on the 4th-and-later targets minus yes-rate on the first target of the run; observed > null means people grow more liberal as they keep answering about the same set (warm-up/anchoring), which the trial-independent model does not produce beyond stimulus differences.
def test_statistic(df):
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ti = df["trial_index"].astype(int)
    new = (ns != ns.shift()) | (ti != ti.shift() + 1)
    blk = new.cumsum()
    pos = df.groupby(blk).cumcount()
    ln = blk.map(blk.value_counts())
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    a = (pos == 0) & (ln >= 4)
    b = (pos >= 3) & (ln >= 4)
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[b].mean() - r[a].mean())

results.name: few_example_far_target_yes_rate
results.description: For sets of 2-3 examples, yes-rate on targets more than 20 outside [min,max] of the examples (excluding targets <=10 and target 100); observed < null means the model over-generalises far beyond the examples' range from few examples (e.g. 28,2 -> 64), i.e. people's generalisation is more magnitude-local than its broad rules imply.
results.code:
# name: few_example_far_target_yes_rate
# description: For sets of 2-3 examples, yes-rate on targets more than 20 outside [min,max] of the examples (excluding targets <=10 and target 100); observed < null means the model over-generalises far beyond the examples' range from few examples (e.g. 28,2 -> 64), i.e. people's generalisation is more magnitude-local than its broad rules imply.
def test_statistic(df):
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",").apply(lambda l: [int(x) for x in l])
    k = sets.str.len().to_numpy()
    mn = sets.apply(min).to_numpy(); mx = sets.apply(max).to_numpy()
    dist = np.maximum(0, np.maximum(mn - t, t - mx))
    m = (k >= 2) & (k <= 3) & (dist > 20) & (t > 10) & (t < 100)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy()
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: small_target_below_range_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate for non-example targets <= 10 that lie below the smallest example; observed < null means the model over-produces downward generalisation to small single-digit numbers (people rarely extend a set to the low end of 1-100).
results.code:
# name: small_target_below_range_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate for non-example targets <= 10 that lie below the smallest example; observed < null means the model over-produces downward generalisation to small single-digit numbers (people rarely extend a set to the low end of 1-100).
def test_statistic(df):
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",").apply(lambda l: [int(x) for x in l])
    mn = sets.apply(min).to_numpy()
    m = (t <= 10) & (t < mn)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy()
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: target_100_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials whose target is 100 and 100 is not one of the examples; observed < null means the model over-produces "yes" to the endpoint 100 (people show an extreme-number aversion that parity/multiples rules containing 100 do not capture).
results.code:
# name: target_100_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate on trials whose target is 100 and 100 is not one of the examples; observed < null means the model over-produces "yes" to the endpoint 100 (people show an extreme-number aversion that parity/multiples rules containing 100 do not capture).
def test_statistic(df):
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    in_set = ex.str.split(",").apply(lambda l: "100" in [x.strip() for x in l])
    m = (t == 100) & ~in_set
    return float(df.loc[m, "rating"].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: shared_digit_any_position_small_sets
results.description: For sets of 2-3 examples, yes-rate on non-example targets that contain (in any position) a digit present in every example, excluding targets that end in a last digit common to all examples; observed > null means people generalise by a shared digit (e.g. 3,31 -> 38; 42,62 -> 28; 68,58 -> 84) far more than the model, whose "contains digit" family gets near-zero prior mass.
results.code:
# name: shared_digit_any_position_small_sets
# description: For sets of 2-3 examples, yes-rate on non-example targets that contain (in any position) a digit present in every example, excluding targets that end in a last digit common to all examples; observed > null means people generalise by a shared digit (e.g. 3,31 -> 38; 42,62 -> 28; 68,58 -> 84) far more than the model, whose "contains digit" family gets near-zero prior mass.
def test_statistic(df):
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",").apply(lambda l: [int(x) for x in l])
    k = sets.str.len()
    common = sets.apply(lambda l: set.intersection(*[set(str(x)) for x in l]))
    lastd = sets.apply(lambda l: {x % 10 for x in l})
    ts = t.astype(str)
    shares = [len(c & set(s)) > 0 for c, s in zip(common, ts)]
    endmatch = [len(c) == 1 and (x % 10) in c for c, x in zip(lastd, t)]
    inset = [x in l for x, l in zip(t, sets)]
    m = (k >= 2) & (k <= 3) & pd.Series(shares, index=df.index) & ~pd.Series(endmatch, index=df.index) & ~pd.Series(inset, index=df.index)
    return float(df.loc[m, "rating"].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: within_set_target_dispersion
results.description: For sets with >= 100 responses, the mean over sets of the standard deviation across targets (non-example, >=5 responses each) of the per-target yes-rate; observed > null means people discriminate among targets within a heavily-probed set (e.g. 52,22,94 -> 16, 44 always yes, 98, 6 mostly no) more than the model, which gives nearly flat predictions across same-parity targets.
results.code:
# name: within_set_target_dispersion
# description: For sets with >= 100 responses, the mean over sets of the standard deviation across targets (non-example, >=5 responses each) of the per-target yes-rate; observed > null means people discriminate among targets within a heavily-probed set (e.g. 52,22,94 -> 16, 44 always yes, 98, 6 mostly no) more than the model, which gives nearly flat predictions across same-parity targets.
def test_statistic(df):
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    cnt = ns.map(ns.value_counts())
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    sets = ns.str.split(",").apply(lambda l: [int(x) for x in l])
    inset = pd.Series([x in l for x, l in zip(t, sets)], index=df.index)
    sub = df[(cnt >= 100) & ~inset]
    if sub.empty:
        return 0.0
    g = sub.groupby([sub["number_set"].astype(str), sub["target"].astype(int)])["rating"].agg(["mean", "size"]).reset_index()
    g = g[g["size"] >= 5]
    sd = g.groupby("number_set")["mean"].std().dropna()
    return float(sd.mean()) if len(sd) else 0.0
